facts.claim: "The Line" by Josiah and the Bonnevilles was released as a single on 2023-05-31.
"The Line" was written and produced by Josiah Leming.
"The Line" is the seventh track on the 2023 album Endurance, which was released on October 25, 2023.
Endurance was self-released and produced and mixed by Josiah Leming, and mastered by Sam Moses.
Leming said he wrote and recorded Endurance in his bedroom studio in Tennessee.
Leming described Endurance as being about the endurance of family, love, pain and, above all, hope.
An instrumental version of "The Line" appeared on Instrumentals Volume 1 on July 5, 2023, with Josiah Leming credited on guitar.
The band name comes from an old Pontiac Bonneville that Leming and Josh Nyback used to drive around the desert.
Leming learned piano at 8 and wrote his first song at 13. As a teenager he lived in his car and toured, which led to a major-label deal at 19. He later released music independently.
In 2026 Josiah and the Bonnevilles signed with Rounder Records. The album As Is, co-produced by Leming and Konrad Snyder, is his first full-length since Endurance.

research.lineage: Sources place the project in Tennessee-rooted folk, Americana and country, with Leming citing his Appalachian heritage and the bluegrass he grew up around.

draft:
The trick of **The Line** is that the narrator gives the whole game away in the first verse. A boundary gets drawn between two hearts, and it sounds sensible until the last line of the stanza: "I do this every time." This isn't a person learning a lesson. It's a ritual, a fence built knowing it's going to be climbed, and Josiah and the Bonnevilles sing it with no alarm at all.

Josiah Leming wrote and produced the song, and it landed on *Endurance*, the record he made in his bedroom studio in Tennessee and described as being about the endurance of family, love, pain and, above all, hope. That last word matters here, because "The Line" is a song about hope the narrator wishes they didn't have. The line is "pretty," and it "Tells me I'll be fine." The self-protection is real, but so is the faint mockery in calling it pretty. The narrator half-knows it's a story told to keep from getting hurt.

Then the chorus admits the pleasure out loud. Hearing someone swear their love is true feels good, and the narrator can't deny it. That honesty sits right next to the hard part: "Bittersweet / Cause it could never come to be." There's no reason given, and none needed. Something makes this impossible, and the feeling shows up anyway, "something so divine." Watch the pronouns, too. The narrator is "wandering across that line," and then the chorus says it's *you* who crosses it. Whose fault is it? The song won't settle it, and the doubled "cross that line" at the end of each chorus sounds less like blame than like surrender.

The second verse tries to argue its way to calm with a run of proverbs: the runner's born to run, wings are made to fly, "I'm old enough to know." It's the voice of someone who has done this before and is reaching for fate to make it hurt less. But the proverbs cut both ways. Maybe the other person is built to leave. Maybe the narrator is.

The sound stays close and small. A fingerpicked acoustic guitar rolls through arpeggios at a slow, easy pace. The lead vocal is breathy with a little rasp, and a second voice comes in high above it on certain phrases. That high harmony over fingerpicking is a quiet nod to the Appalachian and bluegrass music Leming has said he grew up around. The production is clean and clear, with the air of a real room, and nothing is added to dress the feeling up.

It sticks because you know exactly where your own line is, and you know, like this narrator, that you're going to be glad when someone crosses it.
